domainCoverage.synopsis: Proven design idioms that solve recurring structural, behavioral, and architectural challenges with loose coupling and robust resilience.

chapters.title: Dependency Injection
chapters.summary: Dependency Injection (DI) flips object creation inside out: instead of a class instantiating its own collaborators with `new`, an external assembler or IoC container supplies those dependencies through constructors or parameters.

chapters.title: Transactional Outbox Pattern
chapters.summary: The Transactional Outbox pattern eliminates dual-write split-brain by inserting domain events into an `outbox` table inside the exact same ACID database transaction as the business state change, then relaying them asynchronously to Kafka/RabbitMQ.

chapters.title: Circuit Breakers & Resilience Patterns
chapters.summary: A stateful proxy that monitors downstream failures and slow calls over a sliding window, tripping open to fail fast in microseconds instead of letting 2,000ms+ timeouts exhaust caller thread pools.

chapters.title: Bulkhead & Fault Isolation
chapters.summary: The bulkhead pattern partitions shared compute, thread pools, connection pools, and memory into isolated compartments so a slow or failing downstream dependency exhausts only its own quota rather than sinking the entire service.

chapters.title: Sidecar Proxy Pattern
chapters.summary: The sidecar proxy pattern co-locates an independent proxy process (such as Envoy, Vault Agent, or Cloud SQL Proxy) alongside a primary application container inside the same Kubernetes Pod or host, sharing the network namespace and lifecycle. The application talks to `localhost` or transparent `iptables`/eBPF sockets while the sidecar handles TLS termination, auth, retries, and protocol translation.

chapters.title: Leader Election Patterns
chapters.summary: Leader election chooses one coordinator to sequence updates across a cluster while a majority confirms them. It helps replicas maintain one consistent history. The trade-off: failover delays writes and external systems need fencing.

chapters.title: Strangler Fig Migration
chapters.summary: The Strangler Fig pattern incrementally replaces a legacy monolith by intercepting traffic at an edge proxy or gateway, routing specific capabilities to new microservices while keeping existing flows running safely.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Design patterns are battle-tested structural, behavioral, and architectural idioms that decouple software components and resolve recurring system engineering challenges with loose coupling, high cohesion, and runtime resilience. They provide standardized blueprints for managing object lifecycles, isolating fault domains, executing distributed transactions, and guaranteeing idempotency across evolving codebases.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Writing ad-hoc procedural code without structured design idioms leads to rigid, fragile systems where a single requirement change ripples through hundreds of files. In production, unpatterned microservices cascade failures when downstream dependencies slow down, and dual-write operations cause silent data divergence. Mastering structural and resilience design patterns (Circuit Breakers, Bulkheads, Sagas, and Transactional Outbox) is essential for engineering reliable, testable software.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: Design patterns are not intellectual decorations to showcase complexity; they are surgical tools to isolate change, contain failure blast radius, and make distributed workflows recoverable.
coreArchitectureRules: Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software artifacts should be open for extension, but closed for modification. Extend behavior through polymorphism, composition, and strategy patterns rather than mutating stable core classes.

Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level business policies must not depend on low-level technical mechanisms (such as database drivers or HTTP clients). Both must depend on stable abstractions/interfaces.

Composition Over Inheritance: Prefer object composition (has-a relationships) over class inheritance (is-a relationships) to prevent fragile base class hierarchies and encourage flexible runtime behavior swapping.

Resilience Boundary Isolation: Every remote integration must be wrapped in a fault isolation pattern (Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, and Timeout) to prevent transient external outages from crashing the host application.

Transactional Atomicity (Dual-Write Prevention): Never execute a local database write and publish a message broker event in the same code block without a coordinating Transactional Outbox or 2PC pattern.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Inconsistency (Ghost Messages)
failureModes.description: An application writes an order to PostgreSQL and then immediately calls Kafka.send(). If the network drops or the pod crashes before Kafka acknowledges, the order exists in the DB but the event is never published.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement the Transactional Outbox Pattern: save the event into an outbox table within the same ACID database transaction, and tail the outbox asynchronously via Change Data Capture (Debezium).

failureModes.name: Thread Pool Starvation (Unbounded Bulkhead Failure)
failureModes.description: A third-party payment gateway slows down from 50ms to 12,000ms. All incoming application threads block waiting for payment responses, exhausting the shared web server thread pool and halting all other unrelated traffic.
failureModes.mitigation: Isolate external calls with dedicated thread/semaphore Bulkheads and strict 1000ms timeouts, failing fast when the concurrency threshold is breached.

failureModes.name: Circuit Breaker Rapid Flapping
failureModes.description: A circuit breaker transitions from Closed to Open and immediately back to Half-Open on the first success, oscillating repeatedly under flapping downstream conditions and blasting struggling backends.
failureModes.mitigation: Introduce hysteresis and progressive probe testing: require a sustained sequence of consecutive successful canary requests in Half-Open before fully closing the breaker.

failureModes.name: Saga Compensation Cascade Failure
failureModes.description: A distributed checkout saga encounters a failure at step 4, but compensating transactions at step 2 fail due to unhandled exceptions, leaving customer bank accounts debited with no order created.
failureModes.mitigation: Design every compensation step to be strictly idempotent, persistently retried with dead-letter queue escalation, and backed by automated reconciliation jobs.

whenToUse: When system requirements dictate loose coupling between business logic and infrastructure dependencies (storage, third-party APIs, messaging).
Distributed microservice architectures requiring resilient cross-service communications and graceful degradation during network hiccups.
Multi-step business workflows spanning multiple autonomous microservices that cannot use single-database ACID transactions.
Complex domain applications where algorithms or business rules vary dynamically based on customer tier, region, or runtime flags.
whenNotToUse: Trivial CRUD endpoints and internal script utilities where adding interfaces, factories, and strategies creates excessive boilerplate.
Speculative abstraction: creating factory patterns for classes that will only ever have exactly one concrete implementation for the foreseeable future.
Performance-critical inner execution loops where virtual dispatch, interface lookups, and heap allocations add unacceptable nanosecond latency overhead.
Scenarios where simpler functional composition (pure functions and higher-order functions) achieves the same outcome without object-oriented ceremony.

tradeOffs.pro: Sagas eliminate distributed lock contention across microservices, scaling horizontally without blocking database connections.
tradeOffs.con: Sagas require writing complex compensating rollback transactions and sacrifice immediate cross-service isolation (dirty reads are visible during execution).

tradeOffs.factor: Transactional Outbox with Polling vs Change Data Capture (CDC)
tradeOffs.pro: Polling an outbox table with SQL is simple to implement and requires zero external infrastructure changes.
tradeOffs.con: Polling creates database CPU overhead and latency lag; CDC (Debezium) operates at transaction log level with sub-millisecond lag but requires Kafka Connect infrastructure.

tradeOffs.factor: Circuit Breakers: Client-Side vs Mesh Sidecar (Envoy)
tradeOffs.pro: Mesh sidecars (Envoy/Istio) enforce circuit breakers transparently across polyglot microservices without code changes.
tradeOffs.con: Client-side libraries (Resilience4j) have semantic awareness of business exceptions, whereas network proxies only see generic HTTP 5xx codes.

productionScenarios.title: Zero-Data-Loss Financial Outbox at FinTech Unicorn
productionScenarios.scenario: A banking ledger occasionally lost withdrawal notifications when microservice pods were terminated during Kubernetes auto-scaling events right after DB commits.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC streaming Postgres write-ahead logs (WAL) to Kafka, guaranteeing exactly-once event publication and recovering $4.2M in uncollected merchant fees.

productionScenarios.title: Circuit Breaker Protection During Partner API Blackout
productionScenarios.scenario: An international airline booking portal collapsed during an airport partner API outage because 10,000 passenger requests blocked on unresponsive SOAP endpoints.
productionScenarios.outcome: Configured adaptive Circuit Breakers and Bulkhead pools. During partner failure, booking requests degraded gracefully by offering cached flight estimates with delayed ticketing, preserving 99.98% portal availability.

coreChallenges.title: Coupling vs Extensibility (SOLID Principles)
coreChallenges.explanation: Hardcoding concrete dependencies creates tight coupling that makes automated testing and feature swapping painful. Dependency inversion and composition over inheritance preserve flexibility.

coreChallenges.title: Fault Isolation & Resilience Patterns
coreChallenges.explanation: In microservices, a single failing dependency can exhaust thread pools. Circuit breakers, bulkheads, and timeouts isolate failures and enable graceful degradation.

coreChallenges.title: Distributed Transaction Coordination
coreChallenges.explanation: Two-phase commit is brittle in microservices. The Saga pattern coordinates distributed business transactions across multiple services using compensations and local transactions.

coreChallenges.title: Dual-Write Inconsistency & Outbox Pattern
coreChallenges.explanation: Writing to a database and publishing to a message broker in the same operation is non-atomic. The Transactional Outbox pattern guarantees atomic state commits and reliable event delivery.

domainContent.title: Design Patterns

spark.summary: Design patterns are reusable structural, creational, behavioral, concurrency, and integration idioms that isolate variation, enforce clean dependency direction, and keep complex software extensible without rewriting stable code.
spark.keyTakeaway: Patterns are not abstraction trophies; they are targeted seams for isolating what changes from what stays invariant, from in-memory object graphs to asynchronous message pipelines.

domain.purpose: Learn to recognize recurring coupling, lifecycle, concurrency, and integration problems and apply SOLID principles, GoF patterns, and Enterprise Integration Patterns only where concrete variation or failure isolation justifies the indirection.
audience: Software engineers preparing for Low-Level Design (LLD) and object-oriented architecture interviews.
Backend and systems engineers refactoring rigid conditionals, tangled dependencies, or thread-unsafe state.
Technical leads establishing maintainable code boundaries and integration idioms across services.
learningOutcomes: Enforce SOLID boundaries so business rules depend on stable abstractions rather than concrete drivers or SDKs.
Select creational patterns (Factory, Abstract Factory, Builder) to guarantee valid object invariants at construction time.
Compose runtime behavior and adapt incompatible interfaces using Decorator, Adapter, and Proxy without subclass explosion.
Replace brittle conditional branching and tight object-to-object coupling with Strategy, Command, Observer, and Mediator.
Coordinate concurrent execution safely using bounded Producer-Consumer queues, Thread Pools, and Futures.
Design asynchronous integration flows with Pipes and Filters, Content-Based Routers, Aggregators, and Transactional Outbox.

learningJourney.title: SOLID & Object-Oriented Principles
learningJourney.purpose: Establish the five SOLID heuristics that govern class cohesion, safe polymorphism, and dependency direction.
learningJourney.explanation: SOLID principles diagnose why codebases become rigid or fragile. Single Responsibility aligns a module with one actor or reason to change; Open/Closed lets new variants plug in without editing tested callers; Liskov Substitution guarantees subtypes honor caller-visible contracts and invariants; Interface Segregation prevents fat interfaces from forcing dummy implementations; and Dependency Inversion keeps high-level policy independent of low-level I/O.

ideas.title: Liskov Substitution (LSP) is behavioral, not syntactic
ideas.description: A subtype must not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, throw unexpected exceptions, or mutate invariants that callers of the base type rely on. Classic Rectangle/Square inheritance breaks LSP because mutating width silently mutates height.

ideas.title: Dependency Inversion (DIP) flips compile-time coupling
ideas.description: High-level billing or pricing policy defines the repository or gateway interface it needs, and the concrete SQL or HTTP adapter implements it. Policy never imports driver packages.

ideas.title: Interface Segregation (ISP) trims unnecessary recompilation
ideas.description: Splitting a monolithic Worker or Storage interface into narrow role interfaces (Readable, Writable, HealthCheckable) prevents read-only clients from coupling to write-path changes.

example.title: Isolating tax and discount policy from database and ERP drivers
example.scenario: An invoicing module directly instantiated a MySQL connection and a legacy SOAP tax client inside calculateTotal(), making unit testing impossible without a live database and forcing edits to core billing whenever a new tax jurisdiction was added.
example.reasoning: Extracted a TaxCalculator port and InvoiceRepository interface owned by the billing domain (DIP/SRP). Each regional tax rule became an independent implementation registered behind the abstraction (OCP), while read-only reporting consumers depended only on a slim InvoiceSummaryReader interface (ISP).
example.lesson: SOLID turns a single-file tangle of business rules and I/O into testable policy modules with explicit extension seams.

caveats: SRP means one reason to change (one stakeholder/actor), not one method per class.
Prematurely splitting every class behind an interface adds indirection without reducing coupling when only one implementation exists.
reflectionQuestions: Which distinct business actors could force this class to change for unrelated reasons?
Does any subclass violate a precondition, postcondition, or invariant assumed by callers of its parent type?
Are high-level domain policies importing concrete database, HTTP, or filesystem libraries directly?
Which methods on this interface are irrelevant or throwing UnsupportedOperationException for some implementers?

learningJourney.title: Creational Patterns & Object Lifecycle
learningJourney.purpose: Control how complex objects and compatible product families are instantiated while enforcing construction-time invariants.
learningJourney.explanation: Calling `new` directly scatters concrete class names and multi-step setup logic across callers. Factory Method delegates single-product instantiation to subclasses or creator hooks; Abstract Factory produces coherent families of related objects that must match (e.g., UI widgets or cloud storage + KMS clients); and Builder separates step-by-step configuration from validation so immutable objects are never observed partially initialized.

benefits: Decouples caller from concrete product class.
Simple extension hook for creating one product type.
costs: Can lead to parallel creator class hierarchies if overused.

benefits: Guarantees compatible families of objects are created together.
Swaps entire provider suites at startup or configuration time.
costs: Adding a new product type requires updating the factory interface and every concrete family.

benefits: Eliminates telescoping constructors with many optional parameters.
Validates cross-field invariants once in build() and returns an immutable instance.
costs: Extra builder boilerplate for simple value objects with 2-3 fields.

ideas.title: Enforce invariants at build() time
ideas.description: Validate mutually dependent fields (such as minConnections <= maxConnections or non-empty TLS cert when mTLS is enabled) inside build() so invalid configurations fail fast before entering runtime.

ideas.title: Beware hidden global state in Singletons
ideas.description: Classical static Singletons create hidden dependencies and cross-test contamination. Prefer dependency-injected single-instance lifecycles managed by the application composition root.

example.title: Multi-cloud storage client family and HTTP client configuration
example.scenario: A data pipeline needed to switch seamlessly between AWS (S3BlobStore + SqsQueue) and GCP (GcsBlobStore + PubSubQueue), while each HTTP client required 12 optional timeout, retry, and TLS settings.
example.reasoning: An Abstract Factory (CloudProviderFactory) ensured S3 was never paired with PubSub by accident, while a fluent HttpClientConfig.Builder validated that connectTimeout < requestTimeout and produced an immutable config object.
example.lesson: Use Abstract Factory to enforce family compatibility and Builder to guarantee valid, immutable configuration.

reflectionQuestions: Can a caller construct this object in a half-configured or inconsistent state before calling all setters?
Do multiple objects need to match a specific environment or provider family without mixing implementations?
Is a static Singleton hiding dependencies that should be passed explicitly through constructors?
Would a simple static factory method (e.g., Money.of(amount, currency)) suffice instead of a full Factory hierarchy?

learningJourney.title: Structural Patterns: Adapters & Decorators
learningJourney.purpose: Bridge incompatible interfaces and stack cross-cutting behaviors dynamically through object composition.
learningJourney.explanation: Structural patterns assemble objects into larger, flexible structures. Adapter translates an external or legacy interface into the contract your domain expects without polluting domain types. Decorator wraps an object implementing the same interface to layer orthogonal capabilities—compression, buffering, caching, metrics, or retries—at runtime instead of creating a combinatorial explosion of subclasses (CachedBufferedEncryptedStream).

ideas.title: Object Adapter over Class Adapter
ideas.description: Wrapping the adaptee via composition (Object Adapter) works with interfaces, final classes, and runtime-injected instances, whereas multiple-inheritance Class Adapters lock you to a single concrete parent.

ideas.title: Decorator preserves transparency; Proxy controls access
ideas.description: Both wrap the same interface, but Decorator stacks composable enhancements chosen by the caller, whereas Proxy governs lifecycle, lazy loading, access control, or remote dispatch transparently.

ideas.title: Facade simplifies subsystems without hiding escape hatches
ideas.description: A Facade offers a clean high-level entry point over noisy multi-step subsystems while still allowing advanced callers to access underlying components when needed.

example.title: Composable HTTP client middleware and legacy payment SDK adaptation
example.scenario: An e-commerce backend needed to wrap outgoing REST calls with optional retry, rate-limit metrics, and response caching, while integrating a legacy vendor SDK whose method signatures used XML strings and error codes.
example.reasoning: Wrapped the vendor SDK in an Object Adapter implementing the domain's PaymentGateway interface so XML parsing stayed isolated. Implemented RetryClient, MetricsClient, and CachingClient as Decorators around HttpClient, letting each integration compose only the layers it needed.
example.lesson: Compose orthogonal behaviors with Decorators and isolate foreign APIs behind Adapters to avoid subclass explosion and model leakage.

caveats: Decorator ordering matters: placing a CachingDecorator outside a RetryDecorator caches final results, whereas placing Retry outside Caching retries cache misses.
Deeply nested decorator stacks can make stack traces and debugging harder if decorators are not named clearly.
reflectionQuestions: If we have 3 orthogonal features (logging, caching, encryption), how many subclasses would inheritance require vs Decorators?
Where is the boundary that prevents a third-party SDK's types and exceptions from leaking into domain logic?
What breaks if two Decorators in this pipeline are applied in the reverse order?
Are we using a Proxy for access/lifecycle control or a Decorator for caller-chosen feature composition?

learningJourney.title: Behavioral Patterns: Strategy, Command & Template
learningJourney.purpose: Encapsulate varying algorithms, first-class requests, and fixed skeleton workflows without rigid conditional chains.
learningJourney.explanation: When business rules branch on type codes (`if/elif/switch` repeated across files), adding a new variant forces edits everywhere. Strategy extracts each algorithm behind a shared interface so it can be swapped at runtime or injected per tenant. Command reifies an action and its parameters as an object—enabling queueing, scheduling, auditing, and undo/redo. Template Method fixes an invariant multi-step skeleton in a base class while delegating specific steps to hooks.

benefits: Swappable at runtime per request or tenant.
Each algorithm is independently testable with zero base-class coupling.
costs: Callers or a registry must select the right strategy.

benefits: Enforces an invariant step ordering in one place.
costs: Binds variants at compile time via subclassing; harder to mix and match steps.

benefits: Supports persistent queues, retries, undo logs, and macro batching.
Decouples the invoker from knowing how the receiver executes the work.
costs: Requires serializable payloads and inverse state snapshots if undo is needed.

example.title: Dynamic freight pricing and undoable document editor operations
example.scenario: A logistics engine had a 400-line if/else block calculating shipping rates across Ground, Air, ColdChain, and Hazmat carriers, while an internal route planner needed multi-step undo/redo for dispatchers.
example.reasoning: Replaced the conditional tree with a ShippingRateStrategy map keyed by carrier mode, allowing new carrier rules to be added as isolated classes. Modeled dispatcher edits (AssignDriver, ReorderStop) as Command objects pushed onto an undo/redo stack with inverse execute/undo methods.
example.lesson: Use Strategy to eliminate branching over interchangeable algorithms, and Command when invocations themselves must be queued, logged, or reversed.

reflectionQuestions: Are the same switch/if-else branches over a mode or type enum duplicated across multiple methods?
Does the algorithm need to change dynamically at runtime, or is the outer workflow skeleton truly fixed?
Do we need to serialize, queue, rate-limit, audit, or undo individual operations?
In languages with first-class functions, would passing a lambda/function type replace a single-method Strategy class cleanly?

learningJourney.title: Behavioral Patterns: Observer, Mediator & Visitor
learningJourney.purpose: Decouple many-to-many object interactions, prevent observer memory leaks, and add operations over stable object trees.
learningJourney.explanation: Direct references between collaborating components create N-squared coupling webs. Observer decouples a state-changing subject from an open set of listeners, though strong references without explicit unsubscription cause the Lapsed Listener memory leak. Mediator centralizes complex multi-widget or multi-actor coordination into one hub so peers never reference each other directly. Visitor uses double dispatch to add new operations (e.g., type-checking, codegen, serialization) across a stable AST or element hierarchy.

ideas.title: Prevent the Lapsed Listener memory leak
ideas.description: When a long-lived subject holds strong references to short-lived observers, garbage collection cannot reclaim dead UI views or sessions. Always pair subscribe() with explicit unsubscribe(), RAII/disposable tokens, or weak references.

ideas.title: Keep Mediators from becoming God Objects
ideas.description: A Mediator should coordinate interaction rules between colleagues without absorbing each colleague's internal domain logic.

ideas.title: Visitor trades type extensibility for operation extensibility
ideas.description: Adding a new operation (new Visitor) is trivial, but adding a new concrete Element class requires updating every Visitor interface.

example.title: Fixing a memory leak in an order-book UI and coordinating checkout form fields
example.scenario: A trading dashboard leaked 1.2 GB of heap per hour because closed chart panels remained registered on the long-lived MarketFeed subject, while a checkout form had 6 widgets directly mutating each other's enabled/disabled state.
example.reasoning: Returned an AutoCloseable Subscription handle from MarketFeed.subscribe() and used WeakReference cleanup for dropped listeners, eliminating the Lapsed Listener leak. Replaced peer-to-peer widget callbacks with a CheckoutFormMediator that evaluated coupon, shipping, and tax rules in one place.
example.lesson: Observer decouples publishers from subscribers only when subscription lifetimes are bounded; Mediator tames N-to-N peer spaghetti.

reflectionQuestions: If an observer outlives its UI screen or request scope, what mechanism guarantees its subscription is released?
Are N components calling each other directly in a mesh that a single Mediator could simplify?
Is the set of element types stable while operations grow frequently (favoring Visitor), or do new element types arrive constantly?
Could synchronous Observer callbacks trigger re-entrant loops or block the subject's critical path?

learningJourney.title: Concurrency & Threading Patterns
learningJourney.purpose: Structure multi-threaded execution using bounded queues, worker pools, and composable async primitives without deadlocks or OOMs.
learningJourney.explanation: Ad-hoc thread spawning (`new Thread()` per request) exhausts OS stack memory and context-switches CPUs into thrashing. Thread Pools bound concurrency and amortize thread creation; Producer-Consumer pipelines use bounded blocking queues to absorb bursts and apply backpressure when consumers fall behind; and Future/Promise compositions chain non-blocking async stages while propagating cancellation and timeouts.

ideas.title: Never use an unbounded queue in Producer-Consumer
ideas.description: An unbounded queue hides consumer slowdowns until heap memory is exhausted (OOM). Use a bounded BlockingQueue with an explicit rejection or backpressure policy (CallerRuns, drop-oldest, or HTTP 429).

ideas.title: Separate CPU-bound and I/O-bound Thread Pools
ideas.description: Running blocking socket I/O on a small CPU-sized fork-join pool starves compute tasks. Isolate blocking I/O onto dedicated pools or virtual threads/async event loops.

ideas.title: Avoid lock-ordering deadlocks and nested Future blocking
ideas.description: Calling Future.get() inside a worker pool whose tasks submit subtasks to the same pool causes thread-pool starvation deadlock. Chain callbacks (thenCompose) or use separate executors.

example.title: Eliminating thread-pool starvation in an async image-processing service
example.scenario: An upload service used a single shared 32-thread pool where parent tasks called Future.get() on child thumbnail tasks submitted to the same pool. Under burst load, all 32 threads blocked waiting for queued child tasks that could never run.
example.reasoning: Split ingestion and thumbnail rendering into two dedicated pools connected by a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue (capacity 500) with CallerRuns backpressure, and replaced blocking Future.get() chains with non-blocking CompletableFuture composition and per-stage timeouts.
example.lesson: Bounded queues, pool isolation, and non-blocking Future composition prevent thread starvation and memory exhaustion under load.

caveats: Read-Write locks improve concurrency only when reads vastly outnumber writes and critical sections are non-trivial; otherwise lock overhead or writer starvation hurts throughput.
Every async Future/Promise chain needs a timeout and cancellation hook so abandoned requests do not leak work.
reflectionQuestions: What happens to heap memory if producers emit 10x faster than consumers for 5 minutes?
Could a task on this thread pool block waiting for another task queued on the exact same pool?
Are blocking I/O calls sharing an executor with latency-sensitive CPU or event-loop threads?
How does cancellation propagate if the upstream caller disconnects before the Future completes?

learningJourney.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (EIP)
learningJourney.purpose: Compose decoupled messaging pipelines using Pipes and Filters, Content-Based Routers, Splitters, Aggregators, and Dead-Letter Channels.
learningJourney.explanation: Enterprise Integration Patterns standardize how asynchronous systems transform, route, and correlate messages across process boundaries. Pipes and Filters chain independent, stateless transformation stages over message channels; Content-Based Routers inspect headers or payloads to dispatch messages to specialized handlers; Splitters break composite batches into individual items; and Aggregators reassemble correlated replies using a correlation ID and completion timeout.

architectureFlow.name: Ingress Pipe & Schema Filter
architectureFlow.description: Validates envelope schema, assigns a correlation ID, and rejects malformed payloads to a Dead-Letter Channel.

architectureFlow.name: Content-Based Router
architectureFlow.description: Inspects message attributes (region, priority, eventType) to route to the appropriate downstream channel.

architectureFlow.name: Splitter & Parallel Filters
architectureFlow.description: Decomposes batch orders into per-item messages for independent enrichment and validation.

architectureFlow.name: Stateful Aggregator
architectureFlow.description: Correlates enriched items by correlation ID, emits the assembled result, and expires incomplete batches on timeout.

ideas.title: Aggregators require durable state and expiry timeouts
ideas.description: If item 3 of 5 never arrives, an in-memory aggregator without a completion timeout leaks memory forever. Persist partial groups and emit partial/failed notifications on TTL expiry.

ideas.title: Wire Tap and Dead-Letter Channel make pipelines debuggable
ideas.description: A Wire Tap copies messages to an audit/observability channel without altering the main flow, while a Dead-Letter Channel quarantines poison messages so they do not block healthy consumers.

example.title: Decoupling a multi-partner customs & fulfillment pipeline
example.scenario: A cross-border commerce platform needed to validate, enrich, split by warehouse, and reassemble multi-vendor shipments, but a single monolithic processor stalled whenever one carrier API slowed down.
example.reasoning: Refactored the flow into Pipes and Filters over Kafka topics: an enrichment filter normalized addresses, a Content-Based Router dispatched hazardous vs standard items to separate carrier queues, a Splitter fanned out per-warehouse picklists, and a Redis-backed Aggregator with a 30s timeout consolidated tracking numbers.
example.lesson: EIP primitives let each stage scale, retry, and quarantine poison messages independently while preserving end-to-end correlation.

caveats: Every Splitter/Aggregator pair must preserve a unique correlation ID and sequence count across retries.
Idempotent receivers are mandatory because at-least-once messaging channels can redeliver the same message.
reflectionQuestions: Can each Filter stage be deployed, scaled, and unit-tested using only its input and output message schemas?
What happens to an Aggregator's memory if 1% of split child messages are permanently lost?
Where do unparseable poison messages go so they do not trigger infinite retry loops?
How does an operator trace a single business request across 5 asynchronous EIP channels?

endToEndExample.title: Put Design Patterns together: Extensible Payment & Notification Pipeline
endToEndExample.scenario: A SaaS billing engine must support multiple payment providers (Stripe, Adyen, ACH), apply tenant-specific discount/tax rules, emit audit events without dual-write loss, and dispatch webhooks concurrently without starving checkout threads.

architectureFlow.name: PaymentGateway Adapter & Factory
architectureFlow.responsibility: Resolves the tenant's provider via Abstract Factory and translates vendor SDKs behind a DIP-owned PaymentGateway port.

architectureFlow.name: Pricing Strategy & Decorator Chain
architectureFlow.responsibility: Selects regional TaxStrategy and layers Logging, Metrics, and Retry Decorators around gateway calls.

architectureFlow.name: Command & Transactional Outbox
architectureFlow.responsibility: Executes ChargeInvoiceCommand, committing invoice state and outbox event atomically in one local transaction.

architectureFlow.name: EIP Router & Bounded Worker Pool
architectureFlow.responsibility: Content-Based Router dispatches events to Webhook/Email channels consumed by bounded Producer-Consumer worker pools.

reasoning: Dependency Inversion keeps billing domain rules free of Stripe/Adyen SDK types; Object Adapters translate vendor models at the edge.
Builder validates immutable ChargeRequest objects (amount > 0, valid ISO currency) before any provider call is attempted.
Strategy isolates per-country tax and promo rules, eliminating nested conditionals when new markets launch.
Decorator composes idempotency-key injection, latency metrics, and bounded retries without subclassing every provider.
Bounded Producer-Consumer queues and isolated Thread Pools keep slow webhook endpoints from blocking synchronous checkout.
lessons: Each pattern solves a specific structural or operational problem—lifecycle validation, vendor isolation, behavioral swapping, or concurrency bounding.
Composition (Adapters, Decorators, Strategies) scales cleanly where inheritance hierarchies collapse.
Combining local GoF/SOLID boundaries with EIP messaging primitives creates systems that are both easy to unit-test and resilient in production.

failureScenario.title: Slow Webhook Endpoint Starves Checkout Workers
failureScenario.reasoning: A tenant's webhook server stalls for 30 seconds per request. Without bounded queues and pool isolation, notification retries exhaust the shared application thread pool and freeze synchronous invoice charges.
failureScenario.recovery: Isolate webhook delivery behind an EIP Content-Based Router feeding a dedicated bounded Producer-Consumer worker pool with per-request timeouts and a Dead-Letter Channel for repeated failures.

decisionFramework.question: What exact axis of change or coupling are we trying to isolate?
decisionFramework.reason: Introduce a pattern only when concrete variation, lifecycle complexity, or dependency direction demands an abstraction seam.

decisionFramework.question: Can composition (Strategy, Decorator, Adapter) replace inheritance here?
decisionFramework.reason: Object composition avoids fragile base-class hierarchies and allows behaviors to be combined or swapped at runtime.

decisionFramework.question: Are object invariants enforced at construction time?
decisionFramework.reason: Use Builders or factory methods so invalid, half-initialized objects cannot exist in the domain.

decisionFramework.question: Are concurrency and messaging boundaries explicitly bounded?
decisionFramework.reason: Every Producer-Consumer queue, Thread Pool, and EIP Aggregator needs finite capacity, timeouts, and backpressure or dead-letter handling.

decisionFramework.question: Is the added indirection paying for itself in testability and clarity?
decisionFramework.reason: Delete speculative factories or single-implementation interfaces that obscure simple code paths.

knowledgeCheck.question: A notification module currently has a 10-branch switch statement for Email, SMS, Push, and Slack, and you also need optional rate-limiting and audit logging around any channel. Which combination of patterns fits best?

options.text: Create subclasses like RateLimitedLoggedEmailSender and RateLimitedSmsSender for every combination.
options.feedback: Subclassing every channel x feature combination causes exponential class explosion and couples cross-cutting concerns to channel logic.

options.text: Model each channel as a Strategy implementing a NotificationChannel interface, and wrap instances dynamically with RateLimit and AuditLog Decorators.
options.feedback: Correct. Strategy eliminates the switch statement by encapsulating each channel behind one interface, and Decorators compose rate-limiting and logging orthogonally at runtime.

options.text: Put all 10 branches inside a global Singleton Mediator so callers only invoke one static method.
options.feedback: A global Singleton Mediator merely hides the switch statement behind global state without making channels independently extensible or composable.

exercises.title: Refactor a Conditional Pricing Engine
exercises.prompt: Take a monolithic function with nested if/else branches for VIP, Seasonal, Bulk, and Coupon discounts and refactor it using Strategy, Decorator, and a Builder for immutable OrderContext.
reviewQuestions: Can you add a new discount rule without modifying existing pricing classes (OCP)?
Is the order of Decorator/discount application explicit and testable?
Does OrderContext.Builder reject negative quantities or mismatched currencies at build() time?

exercises.title: Fix an Unbounded Producer-Consumer Pipeline
exercises.prompt: An ingestion worker spawns a new thread per event and pushes into an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Redesign it with a bounded Thread Pool, Producer-Consumer backpressure, and CompletableFuture timeouts.
reviewQuestions: What happens when downstream storage stalls for 60 seconds?
Are CPU-bound parsing tasks isolated from blocking I/O tasks?
How are in-flight Futures cancelled on shutdown or timeout?

exercises.title: Architect an EIP Order Enrichment Pipeline
exercises.prompt: Design a messaging flow that accepts batch CSV orders, splits them into line items, routes high-value items for fraud checks, and reassembles completed orders with correlation IDs.
reviewQuestions: How does the Aggregator handle a lost or timed-out fraud-check reply?
Where do malformed CSV rows go without blocking valid items?
Are all Filter stages idempotent under duplicate message delivery?

domainContent.finalSummary: Effective design patterns are pragmatic seams, not ceremony. Ground your code in SOLID dependency direction, favor composition over inheritance, enforce invariants at construction, and bound every concurrency and integration channel.
